title: Participation Is Not Collaboration: When One LLM Coding Agent Reviews Another on GitHub, a Person Answers
description:
Reproducible analysis artifact for the EMSE 2026 Special Issue paper "Participation Is Not Collaboration: When One LLM Coding Agent Reviews Another on GitHub, a Person Answers".

Context: Coding agents such as GitHub Copilot and Devin now open pull requests on their own; we call each a product. Two products on one pull request is often called collaboration, but sharing a page is not answering each other.

Objective: We ask what public path follows one cross-product review comment.

Method: From AIDev, a dataset of agent-authored pull requests, we use three groups: 8,608 pull requests one product reviewed for another (who acts next), 546 matched to a comparable within-product review (does the boundary change the response), and 1,067 still open two days later (does being answered go with merging). Later actions are tied to the comment by GitHub's identifiers, not by timing, and merges are counted only from hour 48, so a reply is seen before the merge.

Results: Direct exchange between products is rare; user accounts take most first actions. Review across the boundary draws 13 points less visible follow-up than its matched within-product twin. A reply that GitHub records as answering the comment goes with 17 points more later merging, and user accounts write four in five of those replies. Yet a reply attached elsewhere does as well, and shuffling the targets barely moves the estimate: the exact link buys attribution, not prediction. Linking an issue roughly doubles the raw answer rate across the boundary and changes nothing inside one product.

Conclusions: Report multi-agent impact as a map of connections, not a count of products. The trace shows human attention, not a resolved review point.

The archive holds the analysis and figure code, the reproduction contract and protocol ledgers, the test suite, the licence files, the README, the citation metadata, a REPRODUCE.md written for someone who has the archive and nothing else, and the derived analysis products under outputs/ that the manuscript tables and figures are built from. MANIFEST.csv and SHA256SUMS cover every file in it.

The AIDev-7.6M release itself is not included. It is third-party data under its own terms and has its own home; the pinned revision is recorded here and in the code so a user can fetch exactly the same one. Also excluded, and asserted on at build time, are the private coder keys and answer keys that would de-blind the human-coding audits, the author-metadata audit, ad-hoc exploration scratch, and the submission-portal staging folder. The MIT licence covers the analysis code, figure code, build scripts, and the derived analysis products. It does not cover the AIDev-7.6M release or any other third-party dataset screened during the external-evidence audit, nor the manuscript text and figures, whose rights transfer is governed by the publisher agreement. See NOTICE.md in the archive.
